extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent applications including statutory authority, formal requisites, searching, making and replying to requirements for information (37 CFR 1.105), interplay with duty of disclosure (37 CFR 1.56), and petitions to expunge information (37 CFR 1.59). Primarily directed to examiner procedure and applicant responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory Authority for Examination / Conditions Precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director shall cause an examination to be made of the application and the alleged new invention; and if on such examination it appears that the applicant is entitled to a patent under the law, the Director shall issue a patent therefor. The main conditions precedent to the grant of a patent to an applicant are set forth in 35 U.S.C. 101, 102 and 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites 35 U.S.C. 131 (examination) and 35 U.S.C. 101 (what is patentable). These statutory provisions are the foundation for examination and for determining entitlement to a patent; examiners must apply 35 U.S.C. 101, 102, and 103 in assessing patentability. (See form paragraph references such as 7.04.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites of the Application
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new application is assigned in the Technology Center, the examiner should review contents to determine if the application meets the requirements of 35 U.S.C. 111(a). Matters affecting filing date or abandonment (lack of oath/declaration, filing fee, or claims) should be checked before storage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must ensure formal matters and completeness/clarity of disclosure per MPEP Chapter 600. If requisites are not met, applicant may be called upon for amendments — but such amendments must not include new matter. Check filing date determinants and whether claims, fees, and oath are present before placing application into storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Obviously Informal Cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When disclosure is informal or insufficient so a complete action on the merits is impractical, follow procedure: make a reasonable search to the extent possible; note informalities and drawing deficiencies; require specification revision to idiomatic English/US practice; reject claims under 35 U.S.C. 112 if informal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifics: (A) reasonable search insofar as invention can be understood (if incomprehensible, state no search made), (B) point out informalities via attachments (MPEP § 707.07(a)), (C) require spec revision to idiomatic English and US practice, (D) reject informal claims for failing to define the invention per 35 U.S.C. 112 (a blanket rejection usually sufficient). Treat multiple obviously informal claims as a single claim for fee and examination. Encourage preliminary amendment within ~3 months to correct obvious informalities but do not permit new matter. Burden is on applicant to revise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Form Paragraphs When Terminology or Disclosure Prevents Proper Search
rubrics_metrics.description: Use form paragraph 7.01 where terminology is such that a proper search cannot be made; use form paragraph 7.02 where disclosure is so incomprehensible that a reasonable search cannot be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph text instructs applicant to clarify terminology/description/correlate with art-accepted terminology and warns against introducing new matter. A shortened statutory period for reply is set (ONE MONTH or THIRTY DAYS, whichever is longer). Examiner notes specify bracketed insertion points (e.g., pages/features not understood) and related MPEP sections for drawing or English problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search Duties and Treatment of Previous Examiner's Search
rubrics_metrics.description: After reading the specification and claims, the examiner searches the prior art; the invention should be thoroughly understood before search. When assigned after actions by another examiner, give full faith and credit to the previous examiner's search and action unless there is a clear error or knowledge of other prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should not take an entirely new approach or perform a new search merely in hope of finding something; see MPEP § 904–904.03 for searching. Informal cases still receive a search to avoid piecemeal prosecution. If a clear error or new pertinent art exists, examiner may revisit prior conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to Require Information under 37 CFR 1.105
rubrics_metrics.description: In course of examining or treating a matter in a pending or abandoned application, patent, or reexamination, the examiner or other Office employee may require submission from individuals identified under § 1.56(c) or any assignee of such information as may be reasonably necessary to properly examine or treat the matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples enumerated by 37 CFR 1.105(a)(1) include: (i) particularly relevant commercial databases known to inventors; (ii) whether a prior art search was made and what was searched; (iii)-(v) copies of non-patent literature/published applications/patents related to the claimed invention or used in drafting or invention process; (vi) identification of what is being improved; (vii) identification of any use of the claimed invention known to inventors at filing. Assignee-held information may also be required when assignee asserted right to prosecute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and Standard for Making a Requirement for Information (Reasonable Necessity)
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a reasonable basis for the information required that would aid in the examination or treatment of the matter. The scope should be narrowly defined and a requirement may be made only when the examiner has a reasonable basis for requiring information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A requirement places substantial burden on applicant and should focus the reason and scope of expected response. It is not a substitute for the examiner performing a search (examiner must search per MPEP § 704.01 and §§ 904–904.03). Criteria generally met where (A) claimed subject matter cannot be adequately searched by class or keyword among patents and typical non-patent sources (e.g., new tech area), or (B) the application file or lack of relevant prior art found justifies asking applicant if he/she has information relevant to patentability. When the applicant is likely to be most knowledgeable (scarcity of art) requiring areas of search is justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of Information Reasonably Required (non-exhaustive list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other examples (not exhaustive) of information that may be reasonably required include: name/citation of relevant indexed journal or treatise; trade name of goods/services embodying claimed subject matter; citations and copies of advertising/promotional literature for such goods/services; journal articles describing such goods/services; trade names/providers of competitors; written descriptions/analyses prepared by inventors/assignees about competing goods/services; identification of pending or abandoned applications by the inventors/assignee disclosing similar subject matter; reply to a protest under 37 CFR 1.291; explanation of technical material in a publication (e.g., inventor’s publication); identification of changes in reformatted continuing applications; mark-up for CIPs showing added subject matter; comments on new Federal Circuit decisions; publication dates of undated documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This list (704.11(a) A–M and others) provides concrete examples of the types of supporting background, commercial, or documentary material that an examiner may reasonably request to properly determine prior art context and patentability. These items are illustrative and not exhaustive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and Appropriateness for Making a Requirement for Information
rubrics_metrics.description: A requirement under 37 CFR 1.105 is discretionary and may be made at any time once necessity is recognized; optimum time is prior to or with a first action on the merits because the examiner can most readily consider and apply the response. Ordinarily a request should not be made with or after a final rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to first action: appropriate where search/preliminary analysis shows claimed matter cannot be adequately searched, e.g., new tech area; factors to consider include whether IDS submitted, adequacy of background, related documents written by inventor/assignee not submitted, references to non-patent literature without copies supplied, admissions in specification unfamiliar to examiner, etc. With the first action: may be combined with a first-action rejection if file or lack of prior art justifies asking applicant. Not appropriate with first-action allowance or Ex parte Quayle. After first action: may be appropriate when file justifies asking applicant, but rarely based on lack of relevant prior art; requirements should generally be in non-final actions because reply must be considered. Under limited circumstances, requirements may be made in issued or abandoned applications (e.g., revival, change of inventorship, reexamination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Replies to a Requirement for Information: Timeliness and Consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Replies to requirements for information must be complete and filed within the time period set including any extensions. Failure to reply within the time period set will result in the abandonment of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All replies should be checked for completeness. Incomplete replies can be completed within the original time period (including extensions). Supplemental replies filed after the original period has expired must comply with other rules for submissions of information. A 37 CFR 1.105 requirement, even absent an action on the merits, is an Office action and is governed by §§ 1.135 and 1.136.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of Requirement for Information (1.105) to Duty of Disclosure (1.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of candor and good faith under 37 CFR 1.56 applies to the applicant’s reply to a requirement for information under 37 CFR 1.105 and requires submission of information reasonably and readily available. The threshold for 1.56 (material to patentability) is substantially higher than that for a 1.105 requirement (reasonable necessity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts: under 1.56 applicant must disclose information material to patentability on his/her own initiative; under 1.105 the Office has authority to require information reasonably necessary to examination, which may not be material to patentability in itself. Applicant must submit information already known but is not required to search for unknown information under 1.105. Information required under 1.105 may include context for state of the art, how invention is practiced, directions of relevant art, and similarities with other art by applicants or assignees.

rubrics_metrics.name: What Constitutes a Complete Reply to a 1.105 Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A complete reply is a reply to each enumerated requirement giving either the information required or a statement that the information required is unknown and/or is not readily available to the party or parties from which it was requested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No requirement that applicant prove the information was not in fact readily attainable, but applicant must make a good faith attempt and a reasonable inquiry once information is requested. A reply stating the information is unknown or not readily available will generally be sufficient unless it is clear the applicant did not understand the requirement or the reply is ambiguous and a more specific answer is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of an Incomplete Reply
rubrics_metrics.description: An incomplete reply to a 37 CFR 1.105 requirement in a pending application or reexamination is handled the same as an amendment not fully responsive to a non-final office action (see 37 CFR 1.135(c) and MPEP § 714.03).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the reply is a bona fide reply, form paragraph 7.95 may be used. Note that a 1.105 requirement, even without an action on the merits, is an Office action; treat procedural handling accordingly (e.g., further action, possible abandonment if not completed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expungement of Information: Petition Standards under 37 CFR 1.59
rubrics_metrics.description: Information in an application will not be expunged and returned except as provided in 37 CFR 1.59(b). Information forming part of the original disclosure (specification including claims, drawings, and any preliminary amendment incorporated into the oath/declaration) will not be expunged. An applicant may request expungement of other information by petition under 37 CFR 1.59(b) with required fee and must establish to the Commissioner's satisfaction that return is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Return of information originally submitted pursuant to MPEP § 724.02 is appropriate where the petitioner satisfies factors (e.g., trade secret/proprietary/unintentional submission causing irreparable harm/not otherwise public/commitment to retain/establishment that info is not material under 1.56/fee). For inadvertently submitted information, petitioner must satisfy criteria including showing unintentional submission and irreparable harm, and include petition fee. Information that is part of the original disclosure is ordinarily not expungable; petitions to expunge original disclosure require an additional waiver under 37 CFR 1.183 and are ordinarily denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling Petitions to Expunge: Procedure and Timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions to expunge under 37 CFR 1.59(b) should generally be held in abeyance until the application is allowed, an Ex parte Quayle action is mailed, or a Notice of Abandonment is mailed; at that time the petition will be decided (TC Director decides if information was submitted under MPEP § 724.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If information was submitted in wrong application, the decision need not be held in abeyance. Where the Office can determine the correct application file, papers may be transferred without a petition. Use form paragraphs (e.g., 7.204, 7.205–7.213) for responses/decisions. If petition granted, expunged material is returned with requirement that applicant retain material for life of any patent issuing on that application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for Granting or Dismissing Petition to Expunge
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions to grant or dismiss a petition to expunge are based on satisfaction of statutory/regulatory criteria and procedural sufficiency (fee, identification, statements). 'Materiality' is defined as any information the examiner considers important to a determination of patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common dismissal reasons/form paragraph headings include: petition lacked required fee (7.207); information is material to determination of patentability (7.208); information has been made public (7.209); no commitment to retain information for life of any patent (7.210); no clear statement that info is trade secret/proprietary/subject to protective order or that submission was unintentional (7.211); failure to clearly identify information to be expunged (7.212); petition not submitted by or on behalf of party in interest who originally submitted the information (7.213). The examiner must explain basis for conclusions when dismissing on materiality or public availability grounds.
